Like the fact that last summer, at the end of her ride, she had seen — briefly, unmistakably — a landscape outside the carousel's rotation that was not the park. She had decided to ride again this summer and pay closer attention.

The carousel began to turn. The park fell away — not dramatically, not with any special effect, simply began to occupy less of her attention than it should, the way a familiar room becomes difficult to recall clearly when you're concentrating on something else. The horse under her was warm in the way that wood in summer is warm, and then warmer, and then warm in a way that wood isn't. The music shifted register. The air smelled different — not the park's cut-grass-and-distant-chips smell, but something older: earth and rain and green growing things in greater quantities than Ashford Park had ever contained. Bea held on tight.

The meadow was real. She knew it was real the way you know certain things — not because you can prove them but because every available sense confirms it simultaneously. The grass was long and dry and rustled against her legs. The sky was the precise blue of a summer afternoon that has been clear all day. The horse was gone and she was standing, which she did not remember doing. In the middle distance a line of trees marked the edge of a wood that she was quite certain had never been in any world she had previously inhabited. She stood still for a moment. Then she began to walk toward the trees.

The wood was old and dense and the light inside it was green and filtered and moved with the trees. She walked for what felt like twenty minutes but might have been less — time inside the wood seemed approximate rather than precise. She found, at the wood's centre, a clearing where a spring emerged from a mossy rock and ran across white stones into shadow. The water was cold enough to ache and the clearest she had ever seen, and when she looked into the spring's pool she saw not a reflection of herself but of the meadow behind her, and in the meadow the horse was waiting. She turned around. It was.

The horse led her to the shore — she hadn't expected a shore, hadn't known the landscape contained one, but it did, black sand and luminous water, the bioluminescence she had read about making the shallow waves glow cold blue-green in what she now realised was dusk. She waded in up to her knees. The light swirled around her feet in slow spirals. Something moved in the deeper water — large, graceful, visible as a shifting density of light rather than a shape. She watched it for a long time. It moved parallel to the shore, neither approaching nor retreating, as if keeping her company from a considerate distance. She raised one hand. The light-shape seemed, perhaps, to pause.

She rode through a city made of glass that caught the remaining light and broke it into spectrum-colours across every surface. The people in it moved through streets that were transparent from below, so the whole city appeared to float. Nobody noticed her — or if they noticed her, they incorporated her into their world the way cities incorporate everything that passes through them: as a passing feature of no particular consequence. She saw a market selling things she had no names for. She saw a library whose shelves went up past any ceiling she could see. She saw a bridge over a canal that was somehow still and moving simultaneously. She tried to memorise all of it.

The mountains were the last place. Stone and cold and the particular silence of high altitude, where the air is thin enough that sound carries differently and you can hear things at great distances with unusual clarity. She climbed — not struggling, not exactly, but aware of each step — until she reached a plateau where the view extended in every direction, the world spread out below in all its variety: the meadow, the wood, the shore, the glass city, the mountains themselves. All of it visible from here. All of it connected. She sat on the cold rock and looked at it and felt the particular vertigo of understanding that something is much larger than you had previously apprehended.

The horse was there when she turned. It always was. She understood now that this was the carousel's logic: you were taken where you needed to go, and the horse returned when you had been there long enough. She mounted and they moved and the mountains dissolved and the park assembled itself around her in the way that dreams dissolve when you wake — all at once, the other world simply no longer present. Mr Voss helped her down. She stood for a moment in the ordinary afternoon light of the park, which was exactly as it had been. She looked at him. 'Where did I go?' she asked. 'Where you needed to,' he said. She looked at her hands. They were cold from the mountain air.

She came back the following summer, and the one after that, and each time the carousel took her somewhere different — somewhere she would not have thought to go on her own, somewhere that left her with something she carried back and couldn't quite explain. Mr Voss was always there, and the music was always slightly different, and the horse was always warm under her hands. She stopped asking where she had been. She started asking, instead, what she had noticed. This turned out to be a better question. Over the years she filled a notebook with what she had seen: the meadow, the wood, the bioluminescent shore, the glass city, the mountains, and places after that she had no words for yet. She kept looking for the words. THE END

books.title: Captain Compass and the Treasure Map
books.description: A young pirate captain follows an ancient map to find friendship, not gold.

pages.text_content: Captain Compass had earned her name honestly. Her compass — a brass instrument that had belonged to her grandmother, and her grandmother's grandmother before that — pointed not just to magnetic north but, on certain days when the light was right and the wind had a particular quality, to something else entirely. Adventure, her grandmother had called it. Captain Compass had always thought this was poetic language. Then one grey morning the compass began spinning wildly on its own, pointing insistently northeast, and she understood that her grandmother had been entirely literal.

She followed the compass through three days of sailing to a harbour town she had never visited, full of narrow streets and the smell of salt and fish and old timber. The compass led her down an alley, around two corners, and into a shop so small and so full that there was barely room to stand. An old sailor sat behind the counter surrounded by the accumulated objects of a lifetime at sea. He looked at her compass without surprise. 'Been expecting you,' he said. 'Or someone like you. Bottom shelf, rolled up, tied with seaweed. Been waiting forty years.'

The map was large and old, drawn on something that felt like neither paper nor parchment but somewhere between the two. The coastlines were precise — she could identify real places in them — but the island marked with the red X had no name and appeared on none of the charts she carried. The turtle shape was unmistakable: a broad oval body, four stubby peninsulas, and a distinctive notch in the top right that could only be the turtle's head. She rolled it carefully back up. She paid the old sailor what he asked without negotiating. Some things were not worth haggling over.

Planning the route took two weeks. The turtle island, triangulated from three separate landmarks shown on the map, placed it in a stretch of ocean she knew only by reputation: technically navigable but poorly charted, subject to unusual currents, and visited rarely enough that no reliable account of its conditions existed. She provisioned the ship carefully — more water than she thought she needed, twice the standard medical supplies, charts of every surrounding area. Her first mate, a cautious man named Boone, looked at the preparations and asked no questions. He had sailed with her long enough to know that questions would be answered in due course.

Twelve days at sea. Three genuine storms, each one different — the first short and violent, the second slow and wearing, the third disorienting in its fog and stillness. She navigated by the old map's landmarks, cross-referencing against her own instruments, finding her way through the poorly charted water with patience and precision. On the eleventh day, Boone called from the lookout. On the horizon, just visible, was a shape — low and broad, with exactly the distinctive outline she had spent twelve days trying to find. Turtle island, exactly as drawn, lying in the morning light like a geographical promise kept.

She rowed ashore in the ship's tender, alone, which Boone protested and she overruled. The beach was white sand, undisturbed except for bird tracks. The vegetation was dense but not impassable. She followed the map's instructions: find the oldest tree visible from the beach, walk toward it, count one hundred paces north from its base, then turn east and walk until you reach flat rock. The oldest tree was enormous, its trunk silver-grey with age. She counted carefully. At one hundred paces: flat rock, exactly as described, half-buried in vegetation, clearly undisturbed for a very long time.

The dig was harder than she expected. The soil beneath the flat rock was dense and full of roots, and the chest was deeper than the map's markings had suggested — nearly a metre down, and heavy. It took two hours and left her thoroughly muddy. When the lid finally opened, she found it lined with oilskin that had kept the interior perfectly dry. Inside were not jewels or gold coins but something she had not expected: fifty maps, each carefully rolled and sealed with wax, each showing a different coastline with a different X, each in the same hand as the first map.

She sat on the beach for a long time, going through them. Each map was clearly genuine — precise coastlines, careful notation, the same quality of observation she had seen in the turtle island map. She recognised some of the coastlines. Others were unfamiliar. Some Xs were marked on islands. Some were on mainland coasts. One was underwater, marked with a depth notation that suggested an extraordinary dive. Each one was a different puzzle, a different journey, a different question waiting to be answered. Her compass, she noticed, had stopped spinning and was now pointing steadily and calmly, as if satisfied.

She returned to the ship as the sun was setting, the chest of maps under her arm, still muddy from the dig. Boone looked at the chest and then at her face and understood without being told that she had found something significant. 'Worth the twelve days?' he asked. She thought about the maps spread around her on the beach — fifty new mysteries, fifty new destinations, a lifetime's worth of questions to answer. 'Worth considerably more than that,' she said. She went below to wash the mud off and start cataloguing. She worked through the night.

By morning she had sorted the maps into categories: coastal, island, underwater, inland. She had identified seventeen that she could navigate to immediately, using routes she already knew. The rest would require planning, new charts, possibly new expertise. The compass sat on the table beside her, pointing steadily northeast — not to any of the maps, she realised, but simply in the direction they had come from. It had done its job. Now the work was hers. She rolled the maps carefully, retied each one, and placed them back in the chest. Then she went on deck, called Boone, and said: 'Set course northeast. I'll explain when we're underway.' THE END

books.title: The Jungle Explorers Club
books.description: Three friends explore a backyard jungle and discover amazing creatures.

pages.text_content: In a cozy village nestled at the edge of the Great Emerald Jungle, there lived three adventurous friends: Maya, Leo, and Anya. The children, with wide eyes full of wonder, often dreamed about the mysteries hidden within the thick, untamed greenery just beyond their backyards. Maya was the keen-eyed observer; she saw things others often missed. Leo, with his boundless energy and courage, was always ready to lead the way. Anya, with her vivid imagination, could conjure stories from the rustle of the leaves or the call of distant birds. Together, they formed the "Jungle Explorers Club," promising to uncover the secrets of the jungle, learn about its creatures, and maybe, if they were lucky, find treasure! Their clubhouse, a small hut they crafted from old crates and draped in a vibrant tapestry of climbing vines, became their world of discovery. Each day after school, they gathered, armed with snacks, notebooks, magnifying glasses, and Maya's prized animal guidebook, planning their next big adventure.

One Saturday morning, excitement buzzed in the clubhouse air. Maya had discovered an old, weathered map tucked inside her great-grandfather's dusty journal. It hinted at a hidden lagoon said to be guarded by exotic creatures and lush flora. The children's eyes sparkled at the prospect of a new quest. “It’s called the Sapphire Lagoon,” Maya explained, pointing at a spot on the map, "and it’s supposed to be full of the bluest water and the rarest birds.” Leo nodded, already imagining the bright colors and cool waters. Anya clutched her drawing pad, ready to capture their discoveries. Eagerly, they packed their bags with essentials: water bottles, snacks, drawing pencils, binoculars, and a small compass Leo had found in the attic. With their hearts racing, they set forth from the village toward the jungle's edge, leaving the familiar dirt paths for the mysterious, green embrace of the wild beyond.

The jungle welcomed them with a symphony of sounds: chirping birds, rustling leaves, and distant calls. The sunlight shattered into a thousand golden beams through the thick canopy, sprinkling the forest floor with warmth. Leo marched ahead, compass in hand, calling out directions like a seasoned captain. Maya flitted from plant to plant, examining unusual leaves and flowers through her magnifying glass. Anya paused often, sketching the twisted trees and vibrant butterflies that flitted by, trying to capture the magic in her scrapbook. As the explorers ventured deeper, the path transformed from a gentle trail to a twisting, overgrown maze. Bushes huddled close, whispering with secrets as they passed. They encountered a family of monkeys swinging above them, watching with curious eyes and mirroring their every move. With little distractions along the way, their excitement grew. What wonders awaited them at the Sapphire Lagoon?

After walking for what seemed like hours, the jungle opened up, revealing a glistening river. The children peered into the clear water, spotting colorful darting fish like underwater jewels. “This must be the River of Glass,” Maya guessed, recalling the name from her guidebook. Leo suggested they follow the river upstream as it seemed to move in the same direction as their map indicated. Along the river’s edge, they came across a fallen log that served as a perfect bridge to cross the river. Holding hands to steady themselves, they made their way across, laughing when Leo almost slipped, but of course, Maya’s quick reflexes came to the rescue. On the other side, giant flowers greeted them, their petals wider than Anya’s arms and colors vibrant as a painter’s palette. Anya eagerly started sketching, each stroke of her pencil trying to capture the grandeur of their new surroundings.

Suddenly, the peaceful jungle echoed with a gentle roar. The children froze, eyes wide with a mixture of awe and fear. From behind a thicket emerged Tico, the friendly tiger, a majestic creature known for his kindness. Leo grinned, relief washing over him. Everyone in the village knew about Tico, the gentle giant with striking amber eyes. “Don’t worry,” Maya whispered to Anya, “Tico is a friend.” The tiger padded towards them, his tail swishing gracefully as he sniffed Leo’s outstretched hand. It seemed Tico, too, was curious about new explorers in his realm. Maya remembered having read that Tico often helped lost wanderers, guiding them through the tangled paths. Anya, feeling braver, sketched Tico’s portrait, capturing his magnificent stripes and soft eyes. With a nod, Tico silently began walking back into the jungle, like a guide leading them further on their unexpected adventure.

Encouraged by Tico’s presence, the children trekked further, closely following the tiger. He led them through narrow, winding paths that seemed as if only he knew their hidden existence. They traversed under arching vines and ducked past hanging branches, their surroundings becoming even more vibrant, with unseen birds singing serenades from above. Soon, the dense jungle gave way to a clearing, bathed in a soft, ethereal glow. There stood the Sapphire Lagoon, shimmering magnificently under the afternoon sun. Its waters sparkled, reflecting the azure sky and flanked by exotic plants with blossoms that looked like stars. Birds with feathers as bright as rainbows danced around, singing a melody as though welcoming the new guests. The adventurers marveled at their enchanted discovery, understanding now why the lagoon’s beauty was hidden away, a treasure for only those bold enough to seek it.

Anya ran forward, dipping her hands into the cool, blue water, laughing at the tickly touch of tiny fish nibbling at her fingers. Leo followed, filling his bottle with some of the water, convinced it must hold special jungle powers. Maya, ever practical, carefully documented their arrival in her notebook, noting every color and sound. As they rested by the water’s edge, a friendly hummingbird, jewel-toned and curious, flitted around them, marking its approval of their presence. “Look!” Anya whispered, pointing to where a family of turtles sunned themselves on a smooth rock, seemingly as old as the jungle itself. The children realized how magical the lagoon truly was – not because it was hidden or guarded, but because of the vibrant life thriving within its embrace. A soft breeze rustled the trees, carrying with it the sweet scent of the blooming flowers, making the adventurers feel at one with the paradise around them.

Soon, Tico nudged Leo gently with his head, a reminder that the day was wearing on and home was a journey away. The children agreed, though their feet wanted to linger longer. As they prepared to leave, Anya proposed they collect a keepsake, a reminder of their enchanting adventure. Maya gathered a fallen flower petal, still velvety and vibrant, while Leo picked a small, smooth pebble from the lagoon’s shore, its surface as clear as glass. Anya finished her sketches as if burning the images into her memory. With a parting glance, the children stepped away from Sapphire Lagoon, following Tico back through the familiar paths that had brought them to this enchanted place. The jungle now seemed like an open book to them, easier to navigate under Tico’s watchful guidance, as though rewarding their bravery with a safe return.

The trek back felt shorter, time slipping by as they reminisced about the day’s wonders and the new stories they would share back at home. Eventually, the silhouette of their village appeared through the trees, warmly welcoming them back with the sight of glowing lanterns marking the path to their clubhouse. Tico paused at the jungle’s edge, bowing his head as if to say farewell. The children hugged him around his massive, soft neck, whispering grateful goodbyes and promises to visit again. Then, with hearts full yet slightly heavy from departing their new friend, the explorers bounded back to their village, chattering about their return journey and how splendid the lagoon had been. Filled with memories and mementos, they couldn’t wait to tell tales of the day’s adventure to their families, ensuring that night’s dinner would be filled with more amazement than ever.

Back at the Jungle Explorers Clubhouse, the children carefully displayed their lagoon treasures on a shelf, where they glistened under the soft glow of their lantern. Anya pinned up her vibrant sketches of the lagoon and Tico, adding bursts of color to the wooden walls. Maya meticulously pasted notes and observations into their shared adventure journal, ensuring every detail was recorded for posterity. Tired but ecstatic, the young explorers celebrated their successful discovery with a small feast of peanut butter sandwiches and fizzy lemonade. As twilight deepened, bringing with it a cool breeze, they promised each other to cherish the memory and begin planning their next grand adventure soon. United by their brave hearts and wild imaginations, the Jungle Explorers Club went to bed dreaming of the untold wonders that awaited them, ready to bring new adventures to life under the ever-watchful eye of the jungle. THE END

books.title: Mountain Climbing Mice
books.description: Brave mice climb the tallest mountain to see the sunrise.

pages.text_content: In a quaint village snuggled between rolling hills and a vibrant, bubbling brook, lived a family of adventurous mice: Milo, the eldest and bravest, Mia, the clever one with twinkling eyes, and Max, the youngest filled with endless energy. Each day, they would scurry through the fields and trees, but from their tiny window, they gaped at the towering mountain looming in the distance. It stood tall and proud, its peak tickling the sky, covered in snow that glittered like a thousand stars in the moonlight. Whispers in the wind spoke of grand adventures and mysteries hidden in its crags, and Milo, with his explorer’s heart, hatched a daring idea. "Let’s climb Mountain Misty," he announced, his whiskers twitching with excitement. Mia and Max exchanged wide-eyed glances, their tiny paws tingling at the thought of the unknown.

With backpacks packed full of crumbs and a thimble of water, the mice set off on their adventure at the break of dawn. The morning sun painted the world in hues of gold and pink, and the meadow they crossed was alive with the soft rustle of waking creatures. They followed a narrow, winding path, lined on either side with wildflowers that danced in the gentle breeze. As they climbed, their little legs worked tirelessly, and Max hummed a cheery tune to keep their spirits high. Each step brought them closer to Mountain Misty, whose grandeur became more palpable with every inch they ascended. The air grew cooler and crisper, invigorating their senses. They marveled at the changes in the landscape, with each rock and crevice promising a story of its own.

By noon, the mice had reached a steep part of the journey, where the path twisted like a tangled vine. They paused for a rest under the shade of an ancient oak tree, its bark rough and comforting against their tiny backs. As they munched on cheese sandwiches, Mia's mind whirred with clever ideas and plans. She suggested they harness a length of silk thread they’d brought with them to assist their climb. Milo nodded approvingly, admiring her ingenuity, while Max bounced on his toes, eager to try it out. With the thread snugly looped around their tiny waists, they felt like seasoned adventurers as they hoisted themselves onto higher ground. The steep climb challenged their stamina, but the promise of reaching the top kept their resolve strong and resilient.

Afternoon shadows crept longer as they climbed, their journey lit by shafts of light that filtered through the foliage. They arrived at a ledge where the view was both breathtaking and humbling. Before them spread a tapestry of emerald fields and silver streams winding through the village they called home. It was a sight so splendid that even chatty Max fell silent. Mia pointed out familiar landmarks that seemed like dollhouse miniatures from this high up. Just then, a gentle breeze ruffled their fur, whispering secrets from the mountain peak. Encouraged by the beauty surrounding them, Milo led them onward, feeling the deep bond of their shared adventure. They were more than mice; they were explorers on a quest, and nothing could stop them now.

Further up the path, the landscape transformed into a rocky terrain dotted with patches of hearty shrubs that bravely clung to life in the harsh environment. Each step was more precarious as loose stones threatened to send the mice tumbling. Milo, always the steady leader, softly coached his siblings, placing paws carefully and ensuring their safety with each movement. Mia’s eyes sparkled as she imagined being the first mouse ever to see the mountain’s secrets firsthand. Max, with uncontained excitement, scrambled ahead with a youthful exuberance that inspired them all. Alongside the challenges, they discovered small wonders — tiny, delicate flowers peeking from crevices, and sparkling dewdrops that clung to the mountain grass like scattered jewels.

With the sun beginning its descent, coloring the sky with streaks of orange and purple, the mice approached a mysterious cave mouth etched in the mountainside. The entrance was cool, like dipping into a shadowy sea, inviting and intriguing. As they ventured in, the cave opened up to reveal walls ablaze with crystals, their shiny, faceted surfaces catching even the slimmest ray of sunlight and casting rainbows around. The awed mice tiptoed inside, their whispers echoing softly across the cavern. Max reached out a paw to touch the crystals, giggling as the cave seemed to sing back to him with every tap. Milo took a moment to reflect on the wonders of nature, feeling a kinship with the world’s ancient spirit, so vividly manifested here.

Pressing on, the mice emerged back into the chilling evening air, where they were greeted by the faint glow of the stars beginning their nightly dance. The path twisted one last time before revealing the summit's final challenge: a gentle slope covered in pure, untouched snow. The mice huddled together for warmth, and with renewed determination, they embarked on the final leg of their journey. Their breath came in visible puffs as the brisk air tickled their noses. The snow crunched underfoot like a symphony of whispers, each step bringing them closer to their goal. As they climbed, the sky unfolded above them, a vast expanse of twinkling constellations that guided their way with celestial precision.

At long last, the brave trio stood victorious at the mountain's peak. The world sprawled before them, a wondrous panorama that stretched to the horizon. They felt as though they had climbed not just a mountain, but into the sky itself, with stars just within reach if only they could leap a little higher. Mia, ever the logical thinker, quietly marveled at how far they’d come, while Max bubbled over with joy, spinning in delighted circles. Milo gazed at the vast world below, cherishing the journey shared with his siblings. Together, they had discovered new perspectives and sparked dreams as grand as the starry sky that enveloped them.

Reluctant to leave but knowing night would soon drape the mountain in darkness, the mice began their descent with hearts full of accomplishment. They moved carefully down the slopes, retracing their steps and sharing memories of their grand adventure. As they passed the familiar landmarks, each stone, and tree became a monument to their bravery. In the cave, they paused to say a fond goodbye to the crystalline wonders, promising to return someday to uncover more of the mountain's secrets. Encouraged by their success, they talked excitedly of future adventures and the wonders that awaited them beyond the horizon. The mountain had taught them not just about its mysteries, but about themselves and their growing courage.

Back in the comforting embrace of their village, the mice were welcomed by the warm glow of their home. All was as they’d left it — the windows framed by the warm light within, and the scent of a late supper wafting through the air. As they snuggled into bed, their hearts were light, filled with the satisfaction of their journey. Wrapped in the warmth of their shared experience, they fell into a peaceful sleep, dreaming of tomorrow’s adventures and the unending sky. Thus, Milo, Mia, and Max discovered that while peaks are tall and sometimes daunting, the view from the top is always worth the climb. Through laughter, discovery, and love, they learned that the most remarkable journeys are those taken together. And so, their dreams soared above the highest mountains, where adventure had no end. THE END.

books.title: The Underground City
books.description: Children discover a hidden city beneath their school playground.

pages.text_content: Fen found the entrance on a Tuesday, which was not a day she associated with extraordinary things, though she conceded afterward that extraordinary things didn't particularly care what day it was. She had been walking the long path through the old hill — a shortcut between the village and the farm that had been used for decades — when she noticed that the crack in the rock face she passed every day was, today, noticeably wider. Wide enough to look into. She looked in. Dark, then less dark as her eyes adjusted, then a tunnel, going inward further than the hill's exterior width could account for. She turned on her phone torch. She went in.

The tunnel went for twenty minutes of walking — slightly downward, gently curving, the walls dry and carved with enough regularity to be clearly not natural. At the end of the tunnel the ceiling abruptly rose and she stepped out into a street. She stood on a pavement of flat cut stones and looked up at carved rock thirty feet above her, and looked along a street of buildings set back behind stone-edged paths, lit by what she would later identify as bioluminescent moss in glass-covered channels running along the walls. Someone passed her, going the other way — small, pale-eyed, with the composed expression of someone going about their day who has seen the occasional surface person before. 'Tourist?' they said. 'Yes,' said Fen. 'This way,' said the small person.

Her guide's name was Silt, and she had been a guide for forty years, long enough to have developed a manner that was efficient without being unwelcoming, informative without being exhausting, and gently corrective of the most common surface-person errors without making them feel inadequate. She showed Fen the street map — carved into the stone at the main junction, detailed and updated regularly — and oriented her. The underground city was called the Underway, and it had been here for five hundred years, and it was organised vertically rather than horizontally, with the deepest levels considered the most prestigious, and it had a population of approximately twelve thousand, and it was, Silt said, generally not secret but not advertised.

The market was the first destination on any tour, Silt said, because it was where you understood most quickly what the Underway was and how it worked. It occupied a natural cavern that had been extended and refined over centuries, and it contained: crystals in every variety and colour, from the functional to the purely beautiful; root vegetables in shapes that grew differently underground than on the surface; fungi of dozens of kinds, some edible and some medicinal and some purely ornamental; carved goods in stone and bone and wood that had to be traded down from the surface; and the fish that had evolved in the Underway's deep lakes, eyeless and pale and moving through the water with the effortless precision of things that had found their perfect medium.

She bought a small purple crystal from a vendor who explained its properties: it held heat for longer than its size should permit and released it slowly, making it useful in cold chambers. She also bought a root vegetable she couldn't identify, which the vendor said tasted of something she would find familiar, and which turned out to taste precisely of butterscotch, which she had not expected but thoroughly appreciated. Silt watched her buy these things with the patient expression of someone who has watched surface people discover the market many times and finds their reactions reliably endearing. 'Most people buy too much on the first visit,' Silt said. 'Because they think they won't come back.' 'Will I come back?' Fen asked. 'Most do,' said Silt.

The district structure of the Underway became clearer as Silt walked her through it. The upper levels were commercial and communal — the market, the guild halls, the schools, the administrative buildings. The middle levels were residential, the homes carved into the rock with varying degrees of elegance and spaciousness. The deep levels — accessed by lifts that used counterweight systems powered by the underground water — were the oldest and most prestigious, some of them occupied by families who had been in the same chambers for two hundred years. 'How do you find new space?' Fen asked. 'You carve it,' Silt said simply. The Underfold were, she added, extraordinary carvers. They had been for five hundred years.

The museum was at the deepest point of the city, as Silt had said it would be, in chambers that were the oldest continuously occupied spaces in the Underway. The exhibits were arranged chronologically: the tools of the first excavation, the founding documents in their original cases, the maps that showed the city's growth from a single tunnel to its current extent. And the founding story, told in painted panels around the walls: the Underfold had not always lived underground. Five hundred years ago, during a long surface winter that had lasted a decade, their ancestors had moved below ground initially for survival and had found something they had not expected — a belonging. They had stayed.

Silt took her to the deep lake on the second level below the museum — a body of water that occupied a cavern so large its ceiling was lost in darkness above them, its surface lit by the bioluminescent organisms that lived in it. The fish were visible from the lake's edge: pale shapes moving in the lit water, their eyeless navigation somehow more purposeful than the seeing kind. Silt said the fish had been adapting to underground life for the full five hundred years of the Underway's existence, and that the biologists in the city tracked their evolution the way surface scientists tracked surface species. 'Five hundred years is not very long,' Silt said. 'But it is enough to begin changing.'

The evening in the Underway was marked by a dimming of the bioluminescent channels rather than a sunset — a shift from the bright active level of day to the softer, warmer level of evening and then the minimal level of night. Fen had been there for six hours. Silt walked her back to the tunnel entrance with the manner of someone completing a satisfactory day's work. She gave Fen a small card — the tourist card of the Underway, with a map on one side and visiting information on the other, including the instruction: Tell no one who would not treat this carefully. Fen looked at the card and then at the entrance and then at Silt. 'What if I want to come back?' she asked. 'Use the entrance you came in,' Silt said. 'It will still be here.'

She emerged into the hillside path in the late afternoon light, the purple crystal in her pocket and the butterscotch root eaten entirely on the walk back through the tunnel. The surface world looked different — brighter, more exposed, the sky improbably large after six hours of stone ceilings. She stood on the path and looked at the hill and thought about the twelve thousand people inside it, going about their days in the carved warmth of the Underway, the fish in the deep lake adapting slowly, the museum at the deepest point holding five hundred years of a people who had found where they belonged. She took out the tourist card. Tell no one who would not treat this carefully. She put it in her pocket carefully, walked home, and began to think about who that might be. THE END

books.title: Sky Pirates of Cloudland
books.description: Flying ships and brave children protect the cloud kingdoms.

pages.text_content: High above the clouds, where the air was thin and cold and the sun was always brilliant, there existed a kingdom called Cloudland. Its islands were made of dense cloud-matter — compressed and solid, enough to build on, to grow things in, to carve roads through — and between them flew the great airships with their canvas sails and their rope ladders and their carved figureheads pointing into the wind. Cloudland had a long history and a complicated politics and, currently, a problem: several of its merchant ships had been robbed on the northern routes, and nobody could work out who was doing it.

The captain of the Zephyr was twelve years old, which was unusual but not unprecedented in Cloudland, where ability counted for more than age in most situations. Her name was Raya, she had seventeen pockets in her coat and charts in eleven of them, and she had been sailing cloud-routes since she was eight. Her crew were: old Finn, who had sailed sixty years and could predict weather by the smell of the air; twins Dash and Dot, who communicated in their own private language and between them could repair anything on a ship; and Policy the parrot, who only ever said 'terms and conditions apply,' which was less useful than it sounded but more useful than nothing.

The Zephyr was painted in seventeen colours applied at different times by different crew members, which gave it a festive appearance that had proved strategically useful — people rarely anticipated anything threatening from a cheerful-looking ship. They had their own code of conduct, posted on the galley wall in Dash's neat handwriting: only take from those who take from others. Return what you recover to whoever it was taken from. Never hurt anyone who isn't actively trying to hurt you first. Keep records. Policy endorsed all of these by saying 'terms and conditions apply' whenever anyone read the list aloud, which everyone had agreed to interpret as approval.

The merchant ship robbery mystery was solved by Dot, who noticed something in the cloud-charts that the merchant captains had missed: every robbery had occurred within two cloud-leagues of a particular navigation marker — a distinctive cloud formation called the Shepherd's Crook — that appeared on every standard chart as a reliable fixed point. 'Someone is using the marker as a waypoint,' Dot signed to Dash. 'They know every ship that uses the northern route passes it.' Dash relayed this to Raya. Raya studied the charts for four hours and then said: 'We need to be there when the next merchant ship passes.'

They positioned the Zephyr in the dense cloud below the Shepherd's Crook and waited. Three days. Finn read the weather in the air — small changes in temperature and pressure that told him things instruments couldn't. On the morning of the third day he said, very quietly, 'Something big coming from the east.' They prepared. An hour later a large grey ship emerged from the clouds — well-armed, flying no flag, moving on a course that would intercept the merchant vessel currently visible on the northern horizon. Raya watched it through her spyglass and made decisions quickly.

The Zephyr's advantage was its speed and its colour scheme. The grey ship's crew, seeing a brightly painted vessel moving to intercept them, made the mistake of assuming it was harmless right up until the moment it wasn't. Raya didn't attack — that wasn't the code. Instead she positioned the Zephyr directly between the grey ship and the merchant, matching the merchant's speed exactly, and opened the signal flags. The message was clear: we see you, we have your description, we know your route. The grey ship altered course. It took twenty minutes of flag signals and two warning shots fired into empty cloud before they backed down entirely.

The recovered goods from previous robberies took longer. They tracked the grey ship to its base — a small private cloud-island not on any public chart — over the following week, following the subtle trail of disturbed cloud-matter that every ship left behind if you knew how to read it. Old Finn knew how to read it. The island had a warehouse, half-full of goods from the merchant robberies, and a crew who, when faced with the Zephyr's reputation and Raya's very specific knowledge of maritime law regarding recovered goods, decided that cooperation was more appealing than the alternative.

Returning the goods took another week — visiting each merchant whose cargo had been taken, documenting the return, collecting the signed receipts that were required by the code. Most merchants were surprised. Several were tearful. One tried to pay a reward that Raya declined on principle, though Policy expressed what seemed like genuine regret about this. At the last merchant's dock, a harbour official appeared and informed Raya that there was a standing offer of a proper commission — a paying job with the Cloudland Merchant Authority — if she and her crew were interested. She said she would consider it. She had not yet considered it when they sailed away.

That evening the Zephyr anchored to a solid cloud-mass and the crew sat on deck watching the sunset — extraordinary up here, where the light came from below as well as above, reflecting off the cloud-sea in shades of orange and pink and deep violet. Finn said it was the finest sunset he'd seen in sixty years. Dash and Dot signed something to each other that made them both smile. Policy said 'terms and conditions apply' in what everyone agreed was a contented tone. Raya sat at the bow with her coat pulled around her and her charts spread on the deck and thought about the commission and about the code and about what she wanted.

She turned the commission down the next morning, sending a polite note by cloud-post. The code said: only take from those who take from others. A commission from the Merchant Authority would mean taking orders from the Authority, and the Authority's interests and the code's interests were not always the same thing. Finn approved. Dash and Dot signed agreement simultaneously. Policy said 'terms and conditions apply' and for once the meaning was very clear. They set course on the northern routes, which still had problems, and the Zephyr's seventeen colours caught the morning light like a flag. Raya stood at the helm and breathed the cold high air of Cloudland and felt, entirely, at home. THE END

books.title: Safari Sam's Big Day
books.description: A young photographer goes on his first safari adventure.

pages.text:
Safari Sam's Big Day

An African Adventure
Today was the day! Sam was going on his very first safari with his grandfather.
They drove across the golden grassland in an open jeep. Sam held his camera tight.
"Look!" whispered Sam. A family of elephants walked by, the baby holding its mother's tail.
Giraffes stretched their long necks to eat from the tallest trees. Sam counted five!
A lion yawned lazily in the shade. "He's taking a nap," Grandfather chuckled.
Zebras galloped past in their stripy pajamas. Sam laughed at how silly they looked!
At the watering hole, hippos and crocodiles shared the cool water peacefully.
As the sun set orange and pink, Sam took one last photo of a beautiful cheetah.

"Best day ever," Sam smiled, his camera full of memories.

The End

books.title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Secret
books.description: A girl discovers her grandfather's lighthouse hides a wonderful secret.

pages.text_content: The lighthouse had been keeping ships safe for a hundred and forty years, and Mrs Blackwood had been keeping the lighthouse for thirty of them. Every evening at dusk she climbed the two hundred and seventeen steps to the lamp room, and every morning at dawn she climbed them again to extinguish the light. Between those times she maintained the mechanisms, polished the lenses, recorded the weather in her logbook, and watched the sea. The sea, she had learned, was always doing something worth watching. You just had to know how to look.

Her grandson Eli came to stay the summer he turned eleven, sent by parents who thought the sea air would do him good and who needed, perhaps, a break from the particular intensity of raising a child who asked more questions than most adults could answer. He arrived with a suitcase of books and a notebook of his own and the immediate conviction that the lighthouse was the most important place he had ever been. He followed his grandmother up the two hundred and seventeen steps on his first evening and watched the lamp light up the dark sea and did not speak, which Mrs Blackwood appreciated.

She taught him the workings: the mechanism that turned the lamp, the lenses that focused the light, the pattern of flashes — three short, one long — that identified this lighthouse to ships that knew how to read it. She taught him the logbook: how to record wind speed and direction, wave height, visibility, the ships that passed. He learned quickly and carefully, writing in the logbook with the neat handwriting of someone who understood that records mattered. On the fourth day she showed him the other logbook — the one she kept in the drawer beneath the regular one, recording different things entirely.

The other logbook recorded the light in the water. She had noticed it on her third year in the lighthouse — a glow beneath the surface on certain nights, blue-green and shifting, moving in ways that had nothing to do with currents or tides. She had researched it extensively. Some of it was bioluminescence, the natural light of sea creatures. Some of it was not. Some of it responded when she signalled with her lamp, flashing back in patterns that were too regular to be coincidence. She had been recording these exchanges for twenty-seven years. She had never told anyone.

Eli watched the water that night with the careful attention of someone who has been trusted with something important. The glow came after midnight — a soft light rising from the deep water beyond the rocks, spreading and shifting, forming patterns that might have been random but felt intentional. Mrs Blackwood signalled with her hand torch: three short, one long, the lighthouse's signature. The glow below responded: three short, one long, and then something else — a longer sequence, a pattern she hadn't seen before. She recorded it in the other logbook. Eli recorded it in his notebook.

They spent the summer mapping the patterns. Eli had the systematic mind that the project required, and between them they began to build a kind of dictionary — recurring sequences and what they seemed to mean, times of night when the glow was brightest, weather conditions that seemed to affect its behaviour. The glow was not random. It was not just bioluminescence. It was, they agreed, communication — though who or what was communicating, and why, remained unclear. The sea kept its secrets. They kept their records.

On the last week of summer, the storm came. A genuine storm, the kind that justified the lighthouse's existence — wind that shook the tower, waves that crashed against the rocks, rain so heavy the beam could barely cut through it. Mrs Blackwood and Eli stayed in the lamp room all night, maintaining the light, watching the weather. Two ships passed, their lights visible in the chaos, guided safely past the rocks by the beam they had kept burning. When dawn came and the storm eased, the sea was full of light — the glow brighter and closer than they had ever seen it.

The light rose to the surface — not just glowing now but forming, taking shape, becoming something that was not quite solid but was definitely present. It stayed for nearly an hour, illuminating the water around the lighthouse rocks, pulsing in patterns that Mrs Blackwood frantically recorded. Then it sank back into the deep and was gone. They sat in the lamp room as the morning sun rose and looked at each other and did not speak for a long time. Some things, Mrs Blackwood had learned, needed to be felt before they could be discussed.

Eli left at the end of summer with his notebook full of patterns and his head full of questions. He came back every summer after that, and every summer they added to their records, building a body of evidence for something they could not explain but could not ignore. The glow continued. The patterns continued. The exchanges continued. They never discovered what was communicating with them or why it had chosen this lighthouse, this keeper, this careful observer. But they kept asking, in the language of light. Some conversations, they understood, were worth having even without answers.

Mrs Blackwood retired when Eli was twenty-three and old enough, she decided, to take over the lighthouse himself. She left him both logbooks — the official one and the other one, now filling its fourth volume. He climbed the two hundred and seventeen steps every evening and every morning, just as she had done, and he watched the sea, and he kept the light burning, and he continued the conversation with whatever was in the water. The sea, he had learned, was always doing something worth watching. You just had to know how to look. And you had to be patient enough to keep looking, even when the answers didn't come. THE END

books.title: Desert Treasure Hunt
books.description: Siblings search for ancient treasure in the sandy dunes.

pages.text:
Desert Treasure Hunt

The Search Begins
pages.text_content: In the vast, shimmering desert, the sun hung like a golden coin in the endless sky. The air was warm and carried the soft scent of sandy dunes mixed with a hint of adventure. Little Maya, feeling a flutter of excitement in her chest, stood on a rocky outcrop, her eyes wide with wonder. Her trusty backpack, heavy with snacks and a folded map, felt secure on her back. Around her, the desert hummed with mysterious sounds—whistling winds and the distant calls of unseen creatures. Her heart pounded with each rustling grain of sand beneath her feet. She glanced at the seemingly endless sea of swirling sand, twinkling under the sun's playful rays, and imagined the treasures hidden beneath. This was the start of something incredible, and Maya's tummy did a little flip of joy at the thought of the treasures that awaited them on this magical desert hunt.

pages.text: Dr. Sara found an old map in her grandfather's journal. X marked a lost tomb!
pages.text_content: In the dusty attic, bathed in streams of soft, golden sunlight filtering through the rafters, Dr. Sara gently opened her grandfather's ancient, leather-bound journal. As she turned the delicate pages that whispered quietly, her eyes sparkled with excitement. Her fingers brushed across a beautifully drawn map, its edges frayed but still vibrant, with a bold red X just beneath a sketch of swirling sand dunes. Beneath the familiar scribbles of her grandfather’s handwriting, a sense of adventure bloomed in Sara’s chest. Her heart raced like a galloping camel in the desert, filled with curiosity and wonder. She imagined the sun-soaked sands stretching endlessly, shadows dancing across ancient stones. The thought of a lost tomb hidden beneath layers of time sent a shiver up her spine, as if the very air whispered secrets meant only for the brave-hearted. It was the beginning of an extraordinary journey!

pages.text: "Let's find it together, Jake!" They packed their gear and headed to Egypt.
pages.text_content: Eagerly, Jake and Lily packed their backpacks, tucking in treasure maps creased from dreaming eyes and a bottle of water each. The golden desert of Egypt called out to them, shimmering under a sun as bright as a thousand lanterns. With each step on the hot sand, they felt the crunch beneath their sturdy shoes. A warm breeze danced around them, whispering secrets of ancient pyramids and hidden treasures with every gust. Jake squinted against the glowing daylight, his heart thudding like a drum with the thrill of adventure. Beside him, Lily grinned, feeling butterflies fluttering in her tummy. Her eyes sparkled with excitement as they imagined the untold mysteries waiting among the sprawling dunes. Everything seemed possible, their friendship as strong as the sunlit pyramids that stood proudly in the distance. As they journeyed on, laughter floated in the air, promising wonders at every twist and turn in the shimmering sands.

pages.text: The desert was hot and vast. But the map led them to ancient ruins.
pages.text_content: The desert stretched endlessly, a shimmering sea of golden sand under the blazing sun. The heat danced in wavy lines above the ground, wrapping around Jason and Lily like a warm blanket, making them squint their eyes. Each step they took left soft, crumbling footprints behind them. The map tucked tightly in Lily's hand, its paper crisp with mystery, promised adventure and hidden secrets. As they trudged through the vastness, a gentle breeze whispered across their faces, carrying the scents of warm earth and dry sage. Their hearts pounded with excitement—a drumbeat of anticipation—when finally, rising like a mirage, they spotted ancient ruins in the distance. Shadows of long-lost columns stood like sentries, whispering stories of time gone by. Jason and Lily’s eyes widened with wonder and a pinch of nervousness, each feeling like brave explorers on the brink of a great discovery.

pages.text: Hidden beneath the sand was a door! Jake spotted the symbols.
pages.text_content: As the hot desert sun beat down on them, Jake suddenly paused mid-step, his heart leaping with excitement. He squinted against the shimmering waves of heat rising from the golden sands. There, barely visible and nestled beneath a thin layer of powdery softness, was a wooden door! The grain of the old wood felt rough beneath his fingers and the air around it was warm, carrying the faint scent of ancient mystery. Peering closer, Jake noticed curious symbols etched deeply into the wood — swirls and circles that enticed his imagination. The endless dunes stretched quietly around him, whispering secrets with each gentle gust of wind. His skin tingled with the thrill of discovery, a smile widening on his face. This was no ordinary door; he could feel it in his bones. What amazing adventures lay waiting just beyond that mysterious threshold? The thought made his heart flutter with anticipation.

pages.text: "These symbols tell a story," Sara explained. "They're the key!"
pages.text_content: Sara's eyes sparkled with excitement as she traced her fingers over the ancient stone. The sun cast playful shadows on the ground, making the symbols dance like mysterious whispers from the past. Each symbol was carved with care, their edges smooth and worn with time. The hot desert breeze rustled around them, carrying grains of sand that tickled Sara's cheeks. Javi stood beside her, his heart thumping like a tiny drum. He could feel a surge of anticipation bubbling inside him, like the fizzing soda on a hot day. The map's secrets felt almost alive in Sara's hands. Together, they sensed the magic of the desert, a tantalizing buzz of adventure wrapping around them like a snug scarf. Amid the quiet stillness, they knew they were about to embark on something truly special, something that would unveil the long-hidden treasure of the desert's golden sands.

pages.text: Inside, they found chambers filled with amazing artifacts!
pages.text_content: Inside the mysterious cave, Max and Lily's eyes sparkled with wonder as their flashlight beams danced across ancient stone chambers, revealing treasures from the past. Everywhere they looked, there were dazzling golden goblets, shimmering in the flickering light like liquid sunshine. Ornate shields leaned against the walls, their surfaces etched with patterns that seemed to tell stories of long ago. The air was cool and smelled slightly of musty earth, making every breath feel like part of a grand adventure. Max felt a shiver of excitement run down his spine, his heart beating like a distant desert drum. Lily’s heart soared with joy, her imagination racing with visions of brave knights and wise queens who once held these very objects. Together, they softly padded over the sandy ground, each step echoing in the vast space like whispers from the past, feeling as though they had discovered a hidden world, all their own.

pages.text: But the real treasure? A library of ancient scrolls - knowledge!
pages.text_content: In the heart of the sunlit cave, where whispers of the wind danced lightly with the quiet shadows, Alex and Mia finally uncovered the real treasure. Their eyes widened in awe as they gazed upon a library of ancient scrolls, each rolled neatly and glowing softly in the golden light. The air smelled of adventure mixed with the faint scent of aged parchment. A gentle hush hung around them, like the cave itself was holding its breath. Alex’s heart thumped with excitement, and Mia's fingers tingled as she reached out, delicately brushing the scrolls that held the secrets of time. They felt an electric thrill, realizing they had discovered something more precious than gold or jewels – a sacred vault of knowledge. The cave seemed to hum a soothing melody, wrapping them in a warm embrace of discovery, making their spirits soar with the magic of a thousand stories waiting to be told.

pages.text: "The greatest treasure isn't gold," Sara smiled. "It's learning!"
pages.text_content: As the warm desert sun began to dip below the horizon, painting the sky in strokes of pink and orange, Sara felt a sense of wonder swell within her. She looked around at the eager faces of her friends, who glistened with sweat and excitement from their day's adventure. The sand was cool beneath their tired feet, a stark contrast to the afternoon’s blazing heat. The gentle whisper of the evening breeze rustled through their hair like playful fingers. More precious than sparkling jewels, their newfound knowledge sparkled in each child’s eyes. They had discovered the secrets of the desert—the way cactus thorns hint at water nestled deep, and how the stars, now twinkling above, form the patterns of stories ancient as time. Sara embraced her friends, feeling the warmth of friendship and the joy of discovery, knowing that this day’s treasure would shine forever in their hearts.

pages.text:
They shared their discovery with the world. History came alive!

The End
pages.text_content: Under the bright, glowing sun, Mia and her brave explorer friends stood on the crest of the sandy dune, their eyes wide with wonder. The shimmering desert stretched far and wide behind them, but now the real magic began. In their hands, they held the ancient amulet, its surface etched with mysterious symbols, sparkling like tiny stars captured in gold. Excitement tingled in their fingertips, and their hearts beat fast with pride. As they shared their amazing discovery with the world, they felt like heroes in a grand story of long ago. History seemed to leap off the pages of dusty old books, filling the air with tales of ancient adventures and secret wonders. Together, they knew their journey had uncovered not just treasure, but stories that would inspire dreamers everywhere. Their sandy footprints marked the beginning of new adventures yet to come, and the desert winds whispered, carrying the promise of excitement on every grain of sand. The End.

books.description: Raccoon friends build a raft and explore down the river.

pages.text:
Kindness Kingdom

Where Good Deeds Bloom
pages.content:
Kindness Kingdom

Where Good Deeds Bloom

pages.text: In Kindness Kingdom, something magical happened whenever someone did a kind deed—flowers would bloom!
pages.content: In Kindness Kingdom, something magical happened whenever someone did a kind deed—flowers would bloom!

pages.text: Princess Kira wore a special dress that changed color with each kind act. Today it was plain white.
pages.content: Princess Kira wore a special dress that changed color with each kind act. Today it was plain white.

pages.text: "How do I fill my dress with colors?" Kira asked Sir Sprout, her sunflower friend.

books.title: The Arctic Expedition
books.description: Young scientists travel to the Arctic to study polar bears.

pages.text_content: The Arctic received Jonas in the way that very large places receive small things: without acknowledgement, without adjustment, continuing whatever it was already doing regardless of his arrival. He stood on the sea ice on the first morning and looked in every direction and saw white — white ground, white horizon, white sky above — with the occasional interruption of pale blue where pressure had fractured and refrozen the ice into ridges. His breath made clouds. The cold was not unpleasant so much as absolute: a fact of the air, total and neutral, treating him and the ice and the distant horizon all the same. He had been told it was beautiful. This was insufficient.

His mother, Dr Sigrid, had been working in Arctic climate research for fifteen years. She had brought him on this expedition partly because he was eleven and old enough and partly because she had been explaining her work to him for five years and had decided he was ready to see it. The research station was small — six scientists, a cook, and now Jonas — on the sea ice north of Svalbard, accessible only by small plane and, for a few months a year, by ship. The station had been measuring the same data points for twenty years. The data told a story. Jonas had read summaries of it. Being here was different from reading summaries.

His job was to help his mother, which meant carrying equipment and writing measurements in the logbook and not falling into any of the cracks in the ice, which were called leads and which his mother had spent considerable time telling him about before they arrived. The ice was not flat. It moved — not visibly, not while you watched, but measurably, over time, drifting on the ocean below it, compressing and separating, thickening and thinning with the seasons. Every measurement his mother took was a data point in a record that stretched back two decades. He understood, writing the numbers, that he was writing sentences in a story that mattered enormously.

The Arctic fox found them on the third day. It appeared at the edge of the station's perimeter with the casual confidence of an animal that owns everywhere it stands, white-coated and bright-eyed, and sat down at a polite distance to observe operations. Jonas sat down at an equally polite distance from it and they regarded each other with mutual interest. The fox had no fear of humans — the station had been here long enough that the local animals treated it as a feature of the landscape — but it maintained its dignified autonomy, coming close enough to satisfy its curiosity and no closer. It visited every afternoon for the rest of their stay.

The polar bear tracks were found on the fifth morning — a mother and two cubs, the prints pressed deep and clear into a patch of softer snow between two pressure ridges. Jonas's mother photographed them and took measurements: the width of the forepaw, the length of the stride, the weight distribution visible in the depth of each print. The bears were somewhere close — the tracks were hours old at most. Jonas stood next to the prints and looked at the white landscape around him, trying to imagine the bears moving through it, invisible in their white coats, going about the urgent business of their lives.

She talked to him about the ice as they worked — not lecturing, just explaining what she was seeing in the way someone explains things they love to someone they trust. The ice had memory, she said. It recorded conditions in its layers — temperature, precipitation, atmospheric composition — the way tree rings recorded growing seasons. A core drilled from deep ice could tell you what the air was like thousands of years ago. She had drilled cores that contained air bubbles from before humans existed in significant numbers. She had measured what was in those bubbles. She knew what the atmosphere had been and what it was now. The difference was the story she spent her life telling.

The Northern Lights came on the seventh night. Jonas was outside for what his mother called star time — the hour before bed when he was allowed to sit outside alone if he was properly dressed and stayed within the station's marked perimeter. He was watching a particularly bright star in the north when the light began: a faint green shimmer at the horizon, barely distinguishable from the sky. Then it strengthened, and broadened, and rose — green deepening to blue-green at the bottom, fading to violet at the top, curtains of light folding and refolding across the sky in slow waves that corresponded to nothing he had ever seen before. He sat completely still.

He understood, technically, what caused it — solar particles exciting atmospheric molecules, the different colours corresponding to different gases at different altitudes. His mother had explained this. Understanding the mechanism did nothing to reduce the experience of it. The lights moved in patterns that seemed almost intentional, though they weren't, that seemed almost musical, though they made no sound, that were simultaneously random and structured in the way that very large natural phenomena always are. He sat under them for forty-five minutes, which was longer than he was supposed to stay out alone, and his mother came and sat beside him without saying anything about the time.

They found the bears on the penultimate morning. A lead had opened overnight — a channel of dark water cutting through the ice — and the mother bear was hunting at its edge, moving with the patient focused attention of something that knows exactly what it's doing. The cubs were nearby, practicing: small clumsy versions of the same careful stalking, occasionally distracted by each other. Jonas and his mother watched from the station with binoculars, not approaching. The mother bear caught a seal with a speed that was shocking after so much patient stillness. The cubs came running. Jonas wrote in his notebook: the patience before the speed. Have to remember both.

On the last day he walked the measurement route with his mother one final time, helping her record the data that would become part of the twenty-year record. He wrote the numbers in the logbook carefully, in his neatest handwriting, because they mattered and because neatness was a form of respect for something important. At the last measurement point his mother stood for a moment looking at the ice, which looked the same as it always looked — white, vast, indifferent — but which she could read as easily as he could read a page. 'It's changing,' she said, not to him exactly, just out loud. He stood beside her and looked at the ice and thought about data points and sentences and stories that needed telling. 'I know,' he said. THE END

The Burping Dragon

A Silly Story

The Burping Dragon

A Silly Story
pages.text_content: In the bustling hallways of Pine Branch Elementary, a peculiar buzz was in the air. It wasn’t just the usual excitement of children chattering or the squeak of sneakers echoing off the shiny floors. No, today was special. As Jazzy clutched her books close, she couldn't shake the feeling of something unusual. Her heart raced with both thrill and a hint of worry as she imagined what might be awaiting in her classroom. Suddenly, the familiar scent of chalk mixed with something unexpected wafted through the corridors—a fruity, bubbly aroma, like someone had unleashed a fizzy lemonade fountain. Upon reaching Room 2B, Jazzy's eyes widened at the sight that greeted her. Sitting right on the teacher’s desk, with emerald scales glistening under the fluorescent lights, was the Burping Dragon! The little dragon burped out a sparkling, golden puff that filled the room with giggles, making Jazzy’s heart flutter with joy and wonder.

pages.text: Burp the dragon had a problem. Every time he tried to breathe fire... BURRRP! Out came a big burp instead!
pages.content: Burp the dragon had a problem. Every time he tried to breathe fire... BURRRP! Out came a big burp instead!
pages.text_content: Burp the dragon had a rather peculiar predicament. Every time he stood in front of his classmates, attempting to impress them with a magnificent fiery display, he focused hard, his scales glimmering like emeralds in the sunlight. His heart would thud with excitement, his nostrils quivering. And then... BURRRP! Instead of roaring flames, a thunderous, amusing belch boomed through the air, echoing against the colorful classroom walls. The other students giggled and clutched their tummies, their eyes wide with delight at the unexpected spectacle. Burp's cheeks flushed a deep shade of crimson, warmer than any fire he had ever hoped to conjure. Although feeling a mixture of embarrassment and amusement, Burp couldn’t help but smile a little, the corners of his mouth curving shyly upwards. Even in his nervous moments, the classroom came alive with laughter, and Burp realized that sometimes, surprise could be just as delightful as fire.

pages.text: The other dragons laughed at him. "What kind of dragon can't breathe fire?" they teased.

pages.text_content: The other dragons gathered in a colorful circle, their scales shimmering like the treasures of a sunset. They erupted into a chorus of giggles that bounced off the tall trees and echoed through the sky. Sam, the smallest dragon, felt a fiery knot form in his belly, not from fire, but from being the focus of all the amusement. The teasing words stung like tiny sparks. His cheeks flushed a warm rose as he stared at his feet, claws tracing patterns in the soft dirt. He wished he could hide behind a puff of smoke. The brave dragons’ laughter sounded like little fireworks popping, but to Sam, it was more like an oncoming storm. He longed to fly away, gentle wings fluttering like leaves, but instead, he stayed, feeling both the cool breeze and the sting of hot tears threatening his eyes.

Frustration crept in as Burp's antennas drooped and his cheeks puffed out. Why couldn't he stop this noisy burbling? The bubbly, giggly snickers of curious classmates drifted from behind corners, making Burp's cheeks turn a shy shade of purple. He needed a solution fast, something to help him stay less, well, burpy!

pages.text_content: One sunny morning, with fluffy clouds lazily drifting across the sky, a brave little knight named Kevin set off on an important quest. His tiny feet crunched on the gravelly path as he made his way to the dragon cave, his heart thumping with both fear and determination. Kevin’s armor clinked and clanked with each step, a shiny silver that gleamed brightly in the sunlight. Inside the dark and cool cave, shadows danced on the stone walls. Kevin felt the cool, damp air brush against his cheeks. He could hear the gentle drip-drip of water echoing in the cave's depths. Though his hands trembled slightly with worry, he stood tall, bravely facing the creature within. In his chest, a flame of hope burned brightly. "Help! A mean ogre is scaring my village!" This tiny knight, with courage as big as a dragon’s roar, sought a powerful friend in this hidden world.

It was the same feeling he felt when he tried new things, like tasting spicy dragonberry jam for the first time. If he was going to help, he had to be brave, and he really wanted to be brave today.

books.title: The Time Machine Treehouse
books.description: A treehouse that travels through time teaches history lessons.

pages.text_content: The treehouse at the end of Cassie's garden had been built by her grandfather thirty years ago and had been ordinary ever since, in the pleasant way of treehouses that are well made and well situated and have been the site of enough childhood activity to have accumulated a quality of use that ordinary things sometimes acquire. Cassie was ten, old enough to spend afternoons there alone, reading or watching the garden below or doing nothing in particular. On the Saturday that everything changed, she had gone up to do nothing in particular and found that the east wall, which she had passed a hundred times without incident, had a brass panel on it that she was quite certain had not been there before.

The panel was approximately thirty centimetres square, set into the wood as if it had always been there, with a small screen, several dials, and a keyboard of unusual configuration. The screen displayed text: TEMPORAL DISPLACEMENT DEVICE. CURRENT LOCATION: GARDEN TREEHOUSE, ASHFORD. CURRENT DATE: DISPLAYED BELOW. DESTINATION: ENTER WHEN READY. The current date was correct. Cassie looked at the panel for a long time. She was ten and sensible and good at mathematics and had read enough science fiction to understand what the panel claimed to be, and she was aware that claiming to be a time machine and being one were different things. She typed: Yesterday. The panel hummed. The treehouse vibrated.

Yesterday was Wednesday, and she arrived in it at 4:17pm, which was when she had been in her bedroom doing homework, visible to herself through the treehouse window at the far end of the garden. She sat very still. The panel had brought her here and appeared to be waiting for her to return, which it had indicated would be required by seven o'clock. She had until seven. She thought about what she wanted to do with this and decided to retrieve the library book she had left on the bus, which was practical and low-risk and would also tell her whether the machine worked in ways that mattered — whether the past was something you could actually interact with, or only observe.

The library book was on the bench at the bus stop, exactly where she had left it. She picked it up. It felt real — paper and cover and the particular weight of a medium-sized novel. She stood at the bus stop with her retrieved library book and thought about what it meant that she could hold this, that she had changed yesterday by being in it. The implications were extensive. She walked home — the past version of her home, where her past self was upstairs doing homework — and returned to the treehouse without going inside, not wanting to complicate things further. Back in the treehouse, she told the panel: Return. It brought her back.

She established rules immediately, before the second journey. Look but don't change — beyond the library book, which was done and could not be undone and seemed, on reflection, too small to have consequences. Don't approach herself or anyone she knew in a way that would be remembered. Document everything. The rules were partly about ethics, which she had thought about carefully, and partly about self-preservation — she understood, even at ten, that changing the past could have unpredictable effects on what came after, and that unpredictable effects in her timeline were something to be careful about. She opened her notebook and wrote: Rule 1.

The second journey was to a year she chose carefully: 1960. Her grandmother had been ten in 1960, and her grandmother had told her once about a particular summer's day — a fete in the village, a specific dress, a memory so clear and present that it had survived sixty years with its details intact. Cassie arrived in the village square in summer sunlight and looked. The fete was there. The dress — described precisely enough that she recognised it — was there, on a girl who would one day be her grandmother, eating candyfloss with the focused attention of someone determined to make it last. Cassie watched from a distance and felt time in a way she hadn't before.

She developed a methodology over the following months. Short visits first — hours rather than days — to understand each period's context before going in further. Research beforehand, using the library and the internet, so she knew what to expect. Notes during, detailed and precise, written immediately on return while the experience was still clear. She visited: the building of the first railway bridge in the area, 1847, standing above the construction site in cold spring light. A storm in 1987 that her father had told her about, watching from the treehouse as it rolled in from the west, enormous and vivid. The field that had existed before the houses, 1920, sitting in open farmland with no road visible in any direction.

The panel disappeared when anyone else climbed up. She had tested this carefully — sending her younger brother up on a pretext, watching from below as he arrived and found only the east wall, the plain wood, nothing brass or anomalous. When he climbed down and she climbed up, it was there. She had thought about telling someone and had concluded that the decision was connected to what the panel's behaviour seemed to indicate: it had found her specifically, and the treehouse's choice to show itself only to her seemed worth respecting. She kept the logbook in a box under the treehouse floor. She told no one.

The most important journey was the last one she would record in the first logbook: to a morning in 1892, specifically to this garden, specifically to the place where the great oak tree stood. She had researched when it was planted — a council record, unexpectedly detailed, gave a date. She arrived in October 1892 and watched a man plant a sapling: very young, barely knee-high, its root ball wrapped in burlap. He was careful with it. He was, she could tell, someone who understood that he was planting something for a future he wouldn't see. She watched him until he was done and then she looked at the sapling, which would become the oak that held her treehouse, and felt the particular vertigo of being in the middle of a very long story.

She was twelve when she filled the first logbook. The second was already half-full. She had forty-nine documented journeys, a methodology that had improved with every trip, and a relationship with time that was different from anyone else's she knew — more layered, more aware of its depth in both directions. She sat in the treehouse on her birthday and opened the panel and looked at the destination field. She had a list of places she wanted to go, carefully researched and prioritised. The list was long enough to occupy years. She looked at the oak tree's branches around her — the oak that a man in 1892 had planted carefully, for someone he would never meet — and thought about all the time that was available, in both directions, if you were paying attention. She typed the next destination. THE END

books.title: Space Station School
books.description: What's it like to go to school floating in space?

pages.text_content: Max sat on his bed, gazing out the porthole of Space Station Starbloom, which hung in the inky darkness like a shiny silver marble. It was his very first day at Space Station School, and excitement buzzed through his entire body like a swarm of tiny comets. The station's artificial gravity made his steps feel bouncy, as if he were made of springs. Outside, the vastness of the twinkling stars looked like sprinkles on a cosmic cupcake, and a distant nebula swirled in colorful splendor. Max's room was tiny but cozy, filled with his favorite things—floating tablets stacked with games and an art kit for drawing alien creatures. Clutching his shiny new backpack covered in galaxy patterns, he took a deep breath of the recycled station air, ready to embark on this otherworldly adventure.

Max's heart raced as he entered the brightly lit corridor leading to the space-bound classroom. The walls shimmered with interactive screens displaying constellations and distant planets.
